sweep_summary: The search of works with stress or accent in the title for Nandi (nand1266) turned up exactly one bibliography item, Downing 2000 'Morphological and prosodic constraints on Kinande verbal reduplication' (Phonology 17:1-38, DOI 10.1017/s095267570000381x). Crossref and the Cambridge Core abstract confirm it is about Kinande, a Bantu language of DR Congo, not Nandi (Southern Nilotic, Kenya); it is a Glottolog mis-assignment under nand1266 (as is Mutaka 1995 'Vowel harmony in Kinande' in the same reference list) and says nothing about Nandi word stress. Paywalled; priority none. No new first-hand Nandi stress statement was read: the on-disk material from the earlier reading (Creider & Creider 1989 Google Books full-text search returns zero hits for 'stress'; Toweett 1975, Kattam 2016, Kipsang 2019 UoN theses; Hyman 2000; Dimmendaal 2012; Lodge 1995; the Pressbooks Nandi profile; archive.org full-text searches) contains no statement of Nandi word-stress placement beyond what the catalog already carries, so the catalog's deciding source (the Harvard library catalogue 1909:156-158, 'all syllables are accentuated alike, a slight stress being perhaps laid on the penultimate', with the modern tonal description from Creider & Creider 1989 via secondary texts) stands unchallenged; catalog_kind 'tonal' is neither confirmed nor contradicted by anything new. the natural next acquisition for a modern first-hand statement remains Creider & Creider 1989 'A Grammar of Nandi' (Buske; print only, HathiTrust catalog blocked by an automated-access block in the the compilation); appended there.

new_statements.quote: Nandi has four tones which must be distinguished in an adequate orthography. An acute accent is used to indicate a high tone. A circumflex accent indicates a high-falling tone. A grave accent marks a low-falling tone, and no accent mark indicates a low tone. The realisation of these tones is as follows: High tone occurs as a rising tone when on a long vowel in initial position [...] the high tone is pronounced on a high level pitch: /ay-we:t/ 'axe'. Low tone occurs as a mid-level tone following a high tone or another mid-level low tone. [...] The tones of words are not stable but are affected by the tones of following [...]

new_statements.relation_note: The catalog lists Nandi with an empty rule (catalog-all-2026-09-12) and no existing stress statements. The dictionary's grammatical introduction supplies the missing classification: Nandi is a four-tone language and the work contains no statement on word stress. Compatible with the empty record; nothing to contradict.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nandi is described as a four-tone language (high, low, high-falling, low-falling; high and low-falling are marked with acute and grave accents, high-falling with a circumflex, low unmarked), with tonal sandhi ('the tones of words are not stable but are affected by the tones of following' words) and tone used grammatically (nominative tone, 'important tonal implications' of an inflection). Nothing is said about word stress: 'stress' occurs exactly once in the whole scanned text, as an English gloss in a verb entry ('2. to emphasise, stress, affirm'), and 'stressed', 'intonation', 'prominence', 'syllable' and 'loudness' return no hits at all when searched together with a phrase unique to the book.
new_statements.exceptions: None about stress. On tone: high tone is realised as rising on an initial long vowel and level elsewhere; low tone is mid-level after a high tone; a high becomes low before another high or a low-falling tone (tone sandhi); some noun forms have first and last tones low and all other tones high.
new_statements.identity_note: The dictionary covers Nandi 'spoken by the Nandi people in the highlands of western Kenya in Nandi, Uasin Gishu (scanned: "Uashin Guishu") and Trans Nzoia Districts'; it refers to Kipsigis as a closely related variety ('such as Kipsigis') but describes Nandi proper. No dialect subdivision is named in the fragments read.

new_statements.relation_note: Agrees with the catalog classification tonal and is the very passage behind the existing verified statement held by the project (Creider & Creider 2001, Introduction p. 15, 'tone language, no stress statement'); it is silent on the Harvard library catalogue 1909's pre-tonal remark of 'a slight stress being perhaps laid on the penultimate', neither confirming nor contradicting it. No new open copy could be found, so the reading still rests on the archive.org search-index fragments, not on a page scan.
new_statements.rule_in_words: Nandi is described as a language with four contrastive tones (high, high-falling, low-falling, low) whose surface realisation depends on vowel length, position and neighbouring tones; the introduction gives orthography, ATR vowel classes, length and tone, and makes no statement about word stress or accent placement (full-text search of the item for stress/penultimate/accented/syllables returns only an English gloss 'to emphasise, stress, affirm' in a verb entry and zero hits otherwise).
new_statements.exceptions: none on stress; on tone: word tones 'are not stable but are affected by the tones of following' words (tonal sandhi), nominative case forms have their own tone pattern ('first and last tones low and all other tones high')
new_statements.identity_note: Nandi proper (Kalenjin), as spoken in Nandi, Uasin Gishu ('Uashin Guishu' in the dictionary's spelling) and Trans Nzoia Districts, western Kenya; the dictionary notes neighbouring Kalenjin varieties such as Kipsigis only for comparison. (Several Glottolog-attached bibliography rows held by the project — Mutaka, Hyman, Black, Downing, Akinlabi — concern Kinande, a Bantu language of DR Congo, not this language.)

sources.quote: "Vowels only have tones in Kipsigiis. There are four main tones in Kipsigiis. The shortening or lengthening of each of these tones may give an impression of another different tone. The Kipsigiis tones (over a) are: Low Tone; High Tone; High-falling Tone; Low-rising Tone (rare)." followed by a chart of disyllabic tonal combinations; nominative marked 'by tonal changes in a word' (the text layer). No statement about word stress or accent anywhere in the thesis.
